---
title: "Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means"
---

## Today's question

We have lengths from 24 seedlings. Twelve independently potted plants were
randomly assigned to a control group and twelve to a treatment group. Each plant
was measured at the beginning and end of the same observation period. Can we
bring the measurements into R without losing their meaning?

Open `introcomputing.Rproj` in the extracted course folder. Its `data/` subfolder
contains the supplied files and a `README.md` explaining them. A **CSV** is a
text file in which commas separate columns. Its first line is a header naming
those columns. The file is storage; importing creates an R object in memory.

## Start from a known place

Create `day07.R` in the project root. Run:

```{r}
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
```

`getwd()` reports R's working directory. It should be your extracted project
folder, not the `data` folder. The second line should return `TRUE`. The relative
path `data/seedlings.csv` means “inside data, find seedlings.csv, starting here”.
Your full home-folder path differs from a classmate's; this relative path can
stay the same when they open their own project.

If `file.exists()` returns `FALSE`, inspect the folder in the file manager. A
common problem is opening the ZIP rather than an extracted project, or an extra
folder layer. Avoid solving this by inserting your personal absolute path into
every line of code. Open the correct project instead.

## Import and inspect

The `readr` package provides a table importer. Packages add functions to R;
installing a package puts it on disk, while `library()` loads it for this session.
The [software setup page](../intro/r-rstudio.qmd) explains installation. Loading is needed again after
restarting R.

```{r}
library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
dim(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
str(seedlings)
```

`read_csv()` returns a table, displayed as a **tibble**. `head()` shows its first
rows, not the complete dataset. `dim()` gives 24 rows and 4 columns. `names()`
returns column names. `str()` describes structure and types: `plant_id` and
`treatment` are text; the two lengths are numeric. Suppressing the type message
with `show_col_types = FALSE` does not remove the need to check types.

Read the first row aloud: plant P01 is in the control group; its initial length
was 25.7 mm and its final length 44.3 mm. Each **row** represents one plant, each
**column** one variable. Two lengths from the same row are measurements on the
same plant, not two independent plants.

```{r}
seedlings$initial_mm
length(seedlings$initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$initial_mm)
```

`$` selects a named column from the table, giving a vector. The length is 24. A
mean without a unit is incomplete: the average initial length is measured in mm.
The numbers cannot tell you whether the file used mm or cm; the dictionary and
measurement protocol provide that information.

## Missing is different from zero

A missing measurement is represented by `NA` after import. `NA` means not
available. It does not mean zero length, no growth, or a control treatment.

```{r}
example_mm <- c(12, NA, 18)
mean(example_mm)
mean(example_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
is.na(example_mm)
```

The first mean is `NA`: R will not silently pretend all measurements are known.
The second is 15 mm, calculated from two observed values. `na.rm = TRUE` requests
omitting missing values for this calculation. A report must still explain how
many observations were missing and why, if known.

## Your practical

1. Import `seedlings.csv` and save the import and inspection commands in `day07.R`.
2. Record in comments the row count, column count, column meanings, and units.
3. Inspect `tail(seedlings)` to see the last rows. Find P24 and its treatment.
4. Use `sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm))` to count missing final measurements.
5. Import `data/leaf-mass.csv` into `leaves`, inspect it, and use its dictionary
   to explain what one row represents. Do not assume it has the seedling columns.
6. Restart R and run your script from the top. The raw CSV files should remain
   exactly as supplied.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: a function is not found

Run `library(readr)` before `read_csv()`. If loading fails because the package is
not installed, use the setup instructions or ask for help. For column names,
copy from `names(seedlings)`; `initial_mm` and `initial` are different names.
:::

## Check your understanding

Why is the header not a plant? Why does the file's name not tell R the units?
Why should the script work from a classmate's project folder?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

The header labels columns rather than containing an observation. Units are
metadata supplied by people; R only sees column names and values. The script uses
relative paths and the same documented folder structure rather than your username.
There are no missing final lengths in the clean seedling dataset.
:::
